In a recent development, the Nike Trail Pegasus 5 has been our top choice for road-to-trail runs for several seasons, so we were concerned that its newly branded replacement, the Nike ACG Pegasus Trail, would mess with its winning formula. But as soon as we stepped into the latest model, we breathed a sigh of relief. The shoe is just as comfortable as its predecessor and, after testing, has proven to be just as capable on and off roads and over gravel, continuing its reign as the most versatile shoe in this roundup.

The midsole foam—Nike’s injection-molded ReactX—feels responsive and cushions comfortably on concrete, pavement, and hard-packed dirt. The outsole traction, from 3.5 mm lugs made of the brand’s proprietary “All Terrain Compound 2.0,” is tackier on wet terrain than the previous version, but still pales in comparison to Vibram MegaGrip.

What makes this shoe work from roads to singletrack trails is the fit and foothold. Even our most narrow-footed testers felt a secure hold without any pressure points, which allows precise footing on trails, no matter how steep or rocky. This shoe’s versatility makes it a great pick as a one-trick pony for the casual runner who doesn’t need a lighter, faster race shoe, and a solid choice for travel.

Weight: 9.5 oz (unisex) Stack Height: 40–34 mm Drop: 6 mm Sizing: 5-12,13 (men’s), 6.5-13.5, 14.5 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Extremely lightweight for a 40 mm stack + Great stability – Premium pricetag.

Industry observers note that brooks has a reputation for building a great shoe and sticking to that formula, giving loyal fans a consistent ride, model after model. The tradeoff? It can make the brand seem boring. The all-new Brooks Cascadia Elite shatters that mold. It’s one of the most exciting shoes Brooks has launched in years, and arguably one of the most exciting trail releases of the year.

Despite sharing a name, the Cascadia Elite is nothing like the everyday, cushioned Cascadia trail runner: It’s a trail racing super shoe that is lighter, faster, and more nimble. The standout feature is the 100% PEBA midsole paired with a carbon-infused PEBAX plate that strikes a perfect balance between a springy and stable ride. On smooth, flowy single track in Santa Barbara, CA, running in the Cascadia Elite felt almost effortless, and a ton of fun.

40 millimeters under the heel is a lot of foam to deal with, but the ride never felt squishy or overly bouncy in off-camber footing. A wide platform, paired with a flexible, embedded horseshoe-shaped plate, keeps the Cascadia Elite from being tippy. That width does come at a cost, though; picking tight lines through technical terrain requires precise footing to keep from getting wedged between rocks.

Sources indicate that if you’re in the market for a trail running shoe, first consider the type of trails you run on regularly: do you tackle rugged, mountainous terrain, or stick to mellow dirt paths? Some trail shoes can handle both adequately, while others are specialized and excel in one or the other. Shoes with smaller lugs are generally better on smoother, firmer terrain, whereas shoes with deeper, more aggressive outsoles are optimized for steep, muddy, or rocky trails. If you like to feel the trail and dance around rocks and roots, you’ll likely prefer a light, more minimal shoe, but if you’d rather let the shoe roll over trail variations, cushioning and protecting while you zone out, you should look for a shoe with a thicker midsole.

Sources indicate that once you’ve narrowed the search to a certain type of trail shoe, you need to find a pair that complements your unique body and stride. Every runner’s body, gait, speed, experience, and ride preferences are different, so every runner will interact differently with each trail shoe. The shoe that your best friend or your sister-in-law loves may be uncomfortable for you and make running feel slow, sluggish, or even painful. Finding the perfect pair of trail running shoes is a seriously personal affair.

The process for choosing the best running shoes is a matter of finding the models that both fit your foot and also feel best when you’re running. To determine fit and feel, there’s no substitute for trying the shoes on and running in them.

Sources indicate that when assessing fit, first pay attention to length. You need room at the end of your toes as your feet lengthen during their dynamic movements on the run. A rule of thumb is to allow a thumb’s width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Runners often wear a running shoe a half or full size bigger than their street shoes.

Ensure that the shape of the sole and the upper matches your foot shape. The sole should be as wide or wider than your foot for the whole length, and match the curve of your arch comfortably. The shoe should hold your foot securely over the instep, while allowing the ball of the foot and the toes to splay and flex when you roll forward onto them. Your heel shouldn’t slip when you lift it, and the arch should be able to dome and lengthen naturally. Nothing should bind or rub as you roll through the stride.

Industry observers note that if the shoe fits, it’s time to take them on a short run on a treadmill, around the store, or, ideally, down the block and back. Every trail running shoe has a unique ride created by the type and density of foam in the midsole and the geometry of that foam: its thickness, width, heel-to-toe drop, molded sidewalls or flares, and forefoot flexibility or rocker shape (plus, in an increasing number of models, the presence of and type of embedded plate). Each of these elements interact with each other and your stride to determine how the shoe reacts on landing, how much it cushions, how stably it supports, how smoothly it transitions from landing to toe off, and how swiftly and powerfully it rebounds.

The best way to choose trail running shoes that complement your body and stride is to find the ones that feel right on the run. Benno Nigg, the world-leading biomechanics professor who proposed this method of shoe selection, calls it the “comfort filter,” but makes clear it is far more than how plush the shoe feels when you step into it. What you want to assess is whether the shoe allows and supports the way your feet want to move, what Nigg calls your “preferred movement path.” In the right shoe, while running at your normal pace, you will touch down where you expect to land, roll smoothly and stably through the stride without noticing the shoe, feel both cushioned from and connected to the ground, and push off naturally, swiftly, and powerfully. When this comes together you’ll know that you’ve found your pair.

It has been revealed that it’s likely that several shoes will feel good on your feet. To find the most comfortable, it helps to compare them back to back, like an eye doctor will do with corrective lenses: flipping between “A” or “B,” “1” or “2.” You may also find that different shoes feel better at different paces or level of fatigue, and you may want more than one pair. In fact, research shows that wearing a variety of different shoes is one of the few proven ways to reduce injury risk as it appears to vary the stresses on your feet and joints.

Recent findings suggest that running shoes have long been marketed and sold as prescriptive devices to help runners stay healthy, but there is little scientific evidence correlating shoes, or any specific shoe properties—like cushioning or pronation control—with running injuries. Medical professionals say that it is highly difficult to determine whether a runner needs a certain type of shoe, and studies have shown that prescribing shoes using traditional methods like treadmill gait analyses or wet-foot arch height tests don’t consistently reduce injuries.

Industry observers note that don’t assume that you need more cushioning or more stability if you have sore joints, or if you’re a heavier runner, or if you’re a beginner—evidence doesn’t support many common beliefs. The best way prevent injury is find two or three different pairs that feel right on the run, ease into using them, and vary your shoes, your running surface and your pace regularly (plus avoid rapid increases in your training load and work on improving your mechanics).

Each season, we evaluate newly introduced releases from top outdoor brands, distributing samples to testers based on foot shape and local trail conditions and preferences. For this fall update, we evaluated 5 new models alongside 91 previously tested shoes to select the best trail running shoes on the market.

According to recent reports, over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across the country (from Santa Barbara to Boulder, Nebraska to Latest Hampshire), our team provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, traction, cushioning, and responsiveness. We combined these reports with our own trail testing to select category winners and top recommendations for every type of runner.

Recent findings suggest that freelance journalist, editor, and author Lisa Jhung has researched, tested, and written about running shoes for the past decade and a half, much of that time for Outside. She coordinates a fleet of female shoe testers out of Boulder, Colorado, and notes her home office is a perpetual obstacle course of cardboard boxes and piles of running shoes. Lisa’s written about gear of all kinds for numerous national magazines as both an editor and freelancer, including a stint as the shoes and gear blogger and trail running microsite editor for Runner’s World.

Industry observers note that A high school jumper and occasional sprinter/hurdler, she started running—really running—after walking off the collegiate volleyball team, and moved on to road and trail races of any distance, triathlons, adventure races, and mountain running. She’s happiest testing rugged trail shoes on gnarly terrain, and also loves a good neighborhood jaunt…but is almost always looking for ribbons of dirt. Lisa is the author of Running That Doesn’t Suck: How to Love Running (Even if You Think You Hate It) and Trailhead: The Dirt on All Things Trail Running.

Cory’s passion for running started over 30 years ago in high school when he became the number six ranked runner in the nation at 3000 meters his senior year. After high school, he competed at Villanova University, earning two NCAA Division I Championship showings. Today, he’s determined not to let age slow him down and competes on the national master’s circuit, running a 4:12 (4:30 mile pace) 1500 meters and 9:04 (4:52 mile pace) 3000 meters in 2021 at age 43. He prefers a hard track workout or tempo run over an easy long run any day but also appreciates a challenging trail or mountain run.

In a recent development, his obsession with running shoes started in 2014 when he wrote his first shoe review for Gear Institute. Since then, he’s tested and reviewed hundreds of running shoes, clothing, and gear for Outside, Runner’s World, Footwear News, and other outlets. He has a soft spot for speedy shoes over heavy trainers but loves dissecting all shoes equally and thinking like a product engineer to explain the why behind every design detail. Cory is the Founder of Run Your Personal Best, an online running coaching business, and since its inception in 2014, has coached runners to over 100 Boston Marathon Qualifying times.

One of Cory Smith’s go-to routes for testing trail running shoes:.

Sources indicate that jonathan fell in love with running his freshman year of high school and quickly became fascinated with finding the perfect pair of running shoes. That quest got a boost when he became editor of Running Times in 2000 and started receiving every new model as they were released. The parade of shoes continued while he served as shoe editor for Runner’s World, then editor of PodiumRunner, and currently fitness gear editor at Outside. Having now worn nearly every running shoe created in this century—and a fair amount of those dating back to the early models of the ’70s—he’s given up on finding the one best and now relishes the wide variety of excellent options.

In a recent development, once a 2:46 marathoner regularly doing 50+ mile weeks, recent injuries and his age have reduced his volume and slowed his pace—but he still enjoys an uptempo workout or two each week. Beverly is the author of the book Your Best Stride which explores how each individual’s gait—and thus shoe preference—is unique. He enjoys getting scientists’ take on fresh shoe trends and trying to describe the nuances of each shoe’s ride.

The Best Cellular Trail Cameras of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for the best overall performance, the Moultrie Edge 4 Solar and Browning Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV share the top spot. For hunters on a budget, the SpyPoint Flex-M2 is the pick. Need maximum detection range, choose the Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0. For the sharpest images, the Stealth Cam Deceptor Max 3.0 leads the field.

In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more.

I’ve been running trail cameras since film-based models were all the rage in the early 1990s. I remember walking laps around the local Walmart, waiting for the one-hour photo lab to process my prints. Most of the time, it was 24 images of a branch that the wind blew back and forth. Occasionally, I’d get a deer—sometimes even a good buck.

According to recent reports, trail cams have come a long way since, and, of course, cellular trail cameras dominate the scene today. If you want to learn all you can about the critters you hunt without setting foot in the woods other than to change batteries or move a camera or two, cellular trail cameras are the way to go. But which cell cams?

Sources indicate that to help you figure out which models are right for you, I spent two months running and testing the latest fresh-for-2026 cell cams in my backyard and on a nearby 700-acre whitetail property in Colorado. Testing conditions were difficult. Every camera was exposed to heavy wind, a 60-day average high temperature of 95.7 degrees, rain, and hail that damaged roofs. The good news: There were no flops. I would have no reservations running any of the new cellular cams below anywhere in the country. That said, some proved better than others depending on what your value most. So, let’s dive in. Here are the best cellular trail cameras of 2026.

Industry observers note that one complaint I’ve always had about cellular trail cameras is the antennas, as they are always breaking off in backpacks or the back seat of my truck. Mother Nature has her way with them, dropping dead branches and crushing skinny, side-mounted antennas. I’ve even broken a couple by catching the antenna in my pant leg while walking to a stand in the dark.

Browning’s Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV features an innovative, wide, blade-style antenna located in the center of the trail camera. It’s extra-sturdy and folds back and locks into the back of the main camera housing for easy, secure transport. The high-gain antenna also grabbed the most available network more promptly than any other camera in this year’s test.

It has been revealed that the MAX HD DV uses the same straightforward interface on the camera’s lower housing behind the lock-and-latch door that Browning users are used to and appreciate. The 1.5-inch LED screen is bright, and the soft-push buttons don’t stick. When you turn the camera on, the LED screen displays a 10-second countdown before you close the door.

Sources indicate that you have plenty of options when setting up the camera via the Strike Fore Wireless app. I recommend running the camera on Medium photo quality with High video. Avoid the Ultra-quality setting for both photo and video to save battery life, as the quality is plenty good without it. All images are delivered in HD, so there are no grainy thumbnails or waiting for the camera to trigger again to view a high-resolution photo. Videos with audio are ultra-clean. The camera took very few false triggers, and I love the user-adjustable flash.

Over 60 days in the field, Browning’s Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV captured deer, day and night, in the center of the frame from 10 feet to 120 feet. Browning lists a detection range of 100 feet, but this camera exceeds that distance.

According to recent reports, using just 8 standard alkaline batteries, camera life was excellent, holding at around 90 percent after 60 days afield. At night, the MAX HD DV uses Illuma-Smart technology to adjust the flash for crisp, clear nighttime images, and its detection range remains over 100 feet after dark. This trail camera was built to handle extreme weather and keep delivering images.

The only area Browning Trail Cameras needs to improve upon is its Strike Force Wireless app. The app functions well but struggles to categorize photos in the main image Library when you’re running more than one camera.

Sources indicate that other than that, Browning’s fresh MAX HD DV is everything I want in a cellular trail camera. It captures HD photos and 1080p video with audio, doesn’t spook deer, and has given me zero hassles after 60 days afield. It’s a tad pricey, but you’ll more than make up for it in batteries.

Moultrie’s Edge 4 Solar is the best solar-powered cellular trail camera I’ve ever used, and, at $169.99—including the solar panel—it is priced right. The panel itself is simple and effective; it slides and locks into the top of the camera, and you can angle the it to ensure it gathers as much sunlight as possible throughout the day.

I’ve had two Edge 4 Solar cameras in the field longer than any other cellular trail camera in this year’s test. They were the first cameras delivered to my doorstep, and when I get a fresh product, I like to start using it right away. Using Moultrie’s $50 (aftermarket) Power Mag II battery pack in tandem with the solar panel, my battery life has never dipped below 80 percent. This means you can stay out of the woods and reduce your human footprint, which is the main goal of cellular trail cameras.

In a recent development, setup is super easy. Like all the trail cameras in this year’s test, the Edge 4 Solar connects to the strongest available cellular network. I like the new internal interface. The white push up/down, on/off button is gone. Moultrie added a twist-and-turn dial that doesn’t stick. The battery life indicator is back, and once powered on, all three lights (Not Connected-red, Connecting-yellow, Connected-green) turn solid. Then, the Connecting light flashes slowly, and after about one minute, the green Connected light turns solid green. At this point, the camera is fully operational. It pairs seamlessly with Moultrie’s app and is one of the most user-friendly cellular trail cameras in this year’s test.

Aside from the new interface, Moultrie made other changes that earned the new Edge 4 Solar our top honor. The most notable is better nighttime image quality and a reduction in false triggers. Moultrie’s new Night Clarity feature uses enhanced low-glow IR LEDs to help illuminate the backdrop and boost edge-to-edge sharpness. Nighttime images are excellent, and every image, day or night, is delivered in HD.

Last year, especially toward the end of my 60-day testing period, my Edge 3 started triggering when nothing was there. The Edge 4 Pro Solar has not followed suit.

Another new and purposeful feature is Buck Shot. Moultrie AI technology detects mature bucks and sends a zoomed-in, max-resolution image. I really enjoyed this feature. Typically, action on my lease doesn’t heat up until mid-October, as few bucks summer on the property. However, this year has been different. A pair of shooter bucks—bucks I passed last fall—are semi-regular on an oat field. The Edge 4 Solar sends me a zoomed-in picture every single time either buck trips the camera.

In a partnership with onX, Edge 4 cameras are instantly pinned the second they are placed. By the end of September, I will have multiple trail cameras—cellular and conventional—spread across the West and Midwest. Too often, I get in a hurry and forget to drop a camera pin when I’m using trail cameras. However, if I’m using Moultrie, I can forget, and the map-pinning technology saves me.

Other standout features of the Edge 4 Solar include a tough-as-nails housing with an IP67 waterproof rating. Both of my Edge 4 Solar cameras have been exposed to torrential downpours and hail. Not a drop of moisture has gotten inside, and after months in the field, the cameras and the panels look like they just came out of the box.

Recent findings suggest that at under $80, SpyPoint’s Flex-M2 is a solid cellular trail camera. It comes with a two-year warranty, and SpyPoint offers a pair of M2s for just $129.99, which is an excellent deal.

My first experience with the Flex-M2 was in Montana while helping a buddy set up his whitetail property. The Flex-M2 is compact, lightweight, easy to set up, and connects to the strongest cellular network in the area. Its .4-second advertised trigger speed proved accurate and reliable in my testing, and the camera captured deer at distances beyond 90 feet.

In a recent development, when I returned from Montana, I added a pair of Flex-M2 cameras to my Colorado property. Both have been on the property for 60 days and send crisp images and 1080p video with solid audio to my phone daily. They have withstood torrid summer heat, rain and hail, and continue to impress me.

According to recent reports, one problem I’ve had with both cameras is battery life. Using standard AA alkaline batteries, both Flex-M2 models drained relatively swiftly. That noted, when I swapped the battery trays for SpyPoint’s LIT-22 rechargeable power packs, battery life improved significantly. Set to Photo-only mode with medium photo resolution and a multi-shot setting of two images per trigger, my battery life has been holding steady above 80 percent.

According to recent reports, setup and connection time was straightforward and quick. I like the positive bottom latch lock, and the raised, gridded on/off switch is easy to operate. Once clicked on, the cellular lights blink until the camera receives a signal. Next, the status light turns blue. Once connected, the blue LED extinguishes, and the green LED on the outside of the camera blinks for 10 seconds. Once the green light stops flashing, the camera is in transmission mode.

The Flex-M2 was the smallest cellular trail cam in this year’s test, and the long antenna is detachable for easy transport. Once you place your M2 in the field, it immediately indicates up on the SpyPoint app map feature.

The camera occasionally produces false triggers, but I was able to reduce this by setting the sensitivity to Medium, and the camera still picks up deer-sized game beyond 90 feet. The BuckTracker feature has done its job. Buck pics are slugged correctly, and I’ve yet to have the technology slug a doe as a buck. BuckTracker even correctly identified and a 3-inch spick at 64 feet.

In the end, Spypoint’s Flex-M2 gets our 2026 Best Value award because while it might not have all the bells and whistles of other cell scouters, it does the job—and does it for about half the price of several others.

Industry observers note that last year, Tactacam’s Reveal Ultra took home top honors in our cellular trail camera test. Its predecessor, the Reveal Pro 4.0, nearly earned the cell-cam maker a repeat performance, but fell just a tad short. It is, however, a cell scouter that every hunter should take a close look at.

Sources indicate that like the Ultra, the Pro 4.0 features Low-Glow and No-Glow flash settings. I love this option. Low-Glow works great for fields, logging roads, or any camera location where detection range needs a bump. No-Glow is ideal for tight timber trail crossings, river crossings, scrapes, or any area where detection range matters less and stealth matters more. The Reveal Pro 4.0 doesn’t spook deer. When set in No-Glow, deer don’t even glance at the camera, and latest Dual Image Sensors improve day and nighttime photos.

Recent findings suggest that another stealth boost is that the slight click that previous Reveal models produced when capturing a nighttime image is gone. According to Reveal, the Dual Sensors—one stacked on top of the other—produce cleaner nighttime images without the audible click associated with a low-light filter. Once you set the Reveal Pro 4.0 in the woods, it’s a ghost, which is just what you want.

In a recent development, battery life on last year’s Ultra model was solid and given that the Reveal app lets owners select camera sensitivity levels between 0 and 9, false triggers have always been few and far between. However, Reveal wanted the Pro 4.0 to have a longer run time, especially when battery-draining features such as larger image sizes, longer video durations, and Live View Mode are used.

Sources indicate that the battery-life boosting answer is Reveal’s FlexPack R5 and R10 Power Systems. The fresh interface location on the camera’s right side, in the upper-right corner, lets the bottom of the camera (the battery box) pull away. The design was well thought out and is an overlooked feature of the new Pro 4.0. With the battery box removed, aftermarket R5 (5,000 mAh) and R10 (10,000 mAh) Power Systems plug in much like rechargeable batteries found on power tools.

Sources indicate that I ran the camera for 15 days using standard Alkaline AA batteries and for 15 days using the FlexPack R5. There is no question the Power Systems increase battery life and are worth the money. During its 15-day run time, the 4.0 with R5 triggered 332 times. I requested 28 videos and purposely activated Live View 10 times to further test battery life. At the end of the test, the camera still had 95 percent battery life remaining.

One small blip with this camera is that of all the cellular models I tested, the Pro 4.0 had the slowest connection time. I ran a pair of Pro 4.0s, and the average time from powering on the cameras to receiving my first test photo in an area with 4 bars of AT&T 5G LTE service was 12 minutes. I’m not sure what that was about, but both cameras struggled to get a signal and start transmitting images. Once the camera were fully connected, though, trigger speed was excellent, detection range was spot-on, and images and videos were clear and colorful.

Industry observers note that if it weren’t for the SpyPoint’s crazy-low price, Stealth Cam’s Deceptor Max 3.0 would have won our Best Photo Quality and Best Value awards. At just under $120, this cellular trail camera should be on every hunter’s radar. Past Stealth Cam cellular models I’ve test produced too many false triggers and had relatively poor battery life. Not so with this one. After 60 days in the field, the Deceptor Max 3.0 has sent only three images to my phone that didn’t show a deer, thanks to the camera’s new False Trigger Filter feature, and after 723 photos and 23 20-second videos, the battery is at 90 percent.

With its No Glow flash, the Max 3.0 has not spooked deer, near or far. Trigger speed is excellent, and with the Command app and the camera set to Standard blur reduction, images have been crisp and clean. The camera captured a doe blazing past at 1:30 a.m. in the center of the frame. The doe was in focus, and 15 seconds later, so were a pair of coyotes hot on her trail.

Industry observers note that the Deceptor Max 3.0 lets users set photo quality to 50MP. That makes for really good pics, but it’s more than most folks need and eats up battery life. I tested the camera at 4MP and 8MP, and the Max 3.0 produced the clearest, brightest, and most colorful images in this year’s test.

In a recent development, A cool feature that Stealth Cam added is Rack Alert, which sends a message to your smartphone letting you know the exact moment a racked deer steps in front of your Max 3.0. This feature worked great on my Colorado lease, and my Oklahoma buddy purchased three Max 3.0 cameras and set them over feeders. He told me he never looks at his image library until Rack Alert informs him. He trusts the technology, and so do I.

Upgraded antenna pulls poor cell service.

The solar cord is big, long, and clunky.

Recent findings suggest that the Interceptor is not newly introduced for this year, but it one of our favorites from last year’s test, winning our Best Trigger Speed award. Covert upped its game 2025, producing a new solar cell cam scouter that’s lightning fast and offers tons of great features. The Interceptor Solar was easy to set up. Downloading the Covert app, building an account, and getting the cam operational took less than five minutes.

According to recent reports, the camera’s paddle-style antenna proved rigid and robust, even in heavy winds. Covert lists the trigger speed at .4 seconds, but my testing showed an average of .24 seconds. That data was obtained using two different stopwatches, as well as a chip time card that runners use.

Industry observers note that when charged to full, the camera’s on-board solar keeps the unit running, even in dense timber. Several times, the Interceptor got down to less than 30 percent battery life at night, but it would still center images in the frame, and deliver good-qualiy photos and real-time 2K video. During the day, even without direct sun exposure, battery life would rise to 80 percent. When set on a pond and alfalfa plot, the battery never dipped below 60 percent and would achieve a full charge during the day.

It has been revealed that covert lists the effective flash range at 90 feet, and my testing confirmed this. I appreciate the 2-inch screen, though very little of the actual setup work is accomplished using the camera. Everything is done in the Covert app. The Covert Interceptor Solar features on-board GPS, so you can’t lose your camera, uses 8 AA batteries as backup, and comes with a 2-year warranty.

In a recent development, my only complaint on this otherwise excellent camera is the long and bulky cord that connects the on-board solar unit to the camera. Be sure to take some Gorilla tape or some zip-ties to roll the cord up and tuck it out of the way. But that’s the end of my quibbling. The camera took only 11 false images during its 20-day testing period and captured a full-sprint coyote in the center of the frame, with no blur. The camera does have species recognition, which works well, but it is a service that costs extra, and I would deactivate it. Like most hunters, I know what a doe and buck deer look like.

Requires a minimum of two cameras.

Longer setup and deployment time.

It has been revealed that cuddeback continues to offer it’s CuddeLink system. The nice thing about Cuddelink is that once you have the Home camera and a cellular initiative, you can run as many as 24 cameras on that same plan, which sarts as low as $10 per month. I opted for the $40 plan to receive unlimited photos. I tested the CuddeLink L-Series Cell Home unit ($130) and CuddeLink L-Seires cell cam ($150), so my initial investment was more. Still, I could add additional CuddeLink-compatible cell cameras (up to 24) to my $40 per month plan.

Operationally, the Home (CuddeLink) and Remote (L-Series) systems are sound. However, you’ll need to read heavy instruction manuals to get them linked to the same chain and go through the settings. It’s not a problem, and it’s not difficult. However, it will take you some time to learn the ins and outs of the system. This duo took much longer to learn about and get in the field than other cameras. That noted, one the initial system is setup, it’s easy to add more cams and daisy chain them into the system.

In a recent development, the CuddeLink L-Series comes in multiple models. I tested the Zoom IR. The photo quality is only decent, but what I do like about the camera is that it uses a center-angle Fresnel lens that increases detection range and zooms the photo in. I’m not in love with having the Home camera and then linking cameras to it, especially cellular, but the system does work and does have the potential to save you money.

Internal screen viewer to aid setup.

Among the most simple setups in the test.

Night pics suffer a bit at longer ranges.

Industry observers note that this camera is not new by any means, but don’t let that stop you. High-quality photos, a lightning-fast trigger, and easy setup are a big pluses with the CelluCore Live. The impressive 0.2-second trigger speed helps capture sharp images and can keep up with fast-moving deer. Plus, the fast image recovery time and subtle infrared flash elevate this cam to the next level. The only thing keeping this camera from the top models is a moderate detection range, and the data plans are, well, not much. It’s not cheap either, though you may be able to find deals.

Industry observers note that thanks to some fantastic friends, I have access to over 700 acres of prime Colorado whitetail dirt, which has proven to be the perfect testing ground for our annual cellular trail camera test. There are plenty of deer to get pictures of and a combination of summer heat, thunderstorms, wind, and extreme temperature fluctuations tests the cameras’ durability.

Since I conducted last year’s cellular trail camera test, I had all the apps on my smartphone. All I did was add cameras, adjust sensitivity levels, check connectivity, and dial in the settings. For testing, I set all cameras to photo resolutions between 4 and 8MP, 1080p video, and two images per trigger.

Before field deployment, I tested all the cams in my backyard. I wanted to make sure they paired with their corresponding app and that photos were transmitting. I set cones at measured distances and walked, jogged, and sprinted past each camera at 10-foot intervals, from 20 to 120 feet. I repeated this process in the field as well. I tested trigger speed and detection zines during daylight and nighttime hours.

According to recent reports, in the field, I rotated all the cameras between four areas: a three-way trail intersection, the lower end of an alfalfa plot, a pond, and a community scrape deer use year-round. Throughout the test—over the course of 60 days—I evaluated each camera’s durability, ease of setup, price, battery life, image and video quality, detection range, and trigger speed. Finally, when all the testing and evaluating is done, I picked our winners.

It has been revealed that ease of setup and quick connection to the camera’s corresponding app save time and frustration. Not every hunter is a tech wizard, and thanks to the simplicity of this year’s camera crop, you don’t have to be. The only camera I had to fight with in terms of connectivity and transmission was the Reveal Pro 4.0. However, that fight was minor.

Many cell-cam makers are skipping grainy thumbnails and going straight to all-HD all the time. I like this. Cell cams have made me very impatient. When I get a picture of a buck, I don’t want to download a grainy image to my computer and then study it for hours trying to determine whether the buck is a shooter while I wait for a high-resolution image to come through. Cams that automatically send hi-res pics get bonus points in my book. Choose a cellular trail camera that lets you adjust image and video quality and set both high enough to avoid compromising image quality but not so high that battery life suffers.

According to recent reports, trigger speed matters, especially during the rut. Many of today’s cellular trail cameras have rapid trigger speed, quicker recovery times, and some type of anti-blur technology. Summertime deer don’t often test a camera’s trigger speed, but during the rut, when a doe comes running past, you want that doe centered in the frame, and the camera needs to recover fast enough that the big buck hot on her heels gets his picture taken too. The cellular trail cameras I tested this year have fast triggers and quick recovery times.

I prefer cellular trail cameras with an adjustable flash. Some come with adjustable flash settings, while others adjust the flash setting automatically based on the time of day. Stay away from high-glow LEDs and any cell camera that produces a flash that spooks deer. All the cameras I tested this year didn’t bother deer a bit.

Sources indicate that cellular trail-cam manufacturers embellish a lot of things. One thing they don’t embellish—or at least didn’t embellish this year, is detection range. If anything, they underplayed it. Detection range is the maximum distance at which a camera will detect an object. Typically, the farther an object is from the camera, the larger it needs to be to be detected by the camera. Anything at over 100 feet is impressive.

It has been revealed that I like a very basic and straightforward app that allows me immediate access to the camera’s settings. I like to try all the technologies and features of every cell camera I test. The better the app, the easier it is to swap between settings, organize photos, etc. Many of today’s cellular trail cameras have fancy features. Take advantage of them and see if you find them beneficial. Some of them drain battery life; others don’t. Find out what works best for you and the area you hunt.

Tech Report: Budget Ski Gear Is Hiding at Costco, and Some of It Is From Brands We Trust

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Industry observers note that you don’t need to pay premium prices to build a ski-day layering system.
  • Sources indicate that overview: These editor-approved Costco ski gear picks come from brands skiers know, like Smith, Spyder, Head, and Dakine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Industry observers note that you don’t need to pay premium prices to build a ski-day layering system. (Photo: Re Wikstrom).

Sources indicate that overview: These editor-approved Costco ski gear picks come from brands skiers know, like Smith, Spyder, Head, and Dakine. We flag what you give up at each price, so beginners and casual skiers can shop smart. Skiers facing harsh weather may still want premium shells and insulation. Costco’s stock changes fast, so grab what you want early.

Sources indicate that with groceries and gas so pricey, it’s no wonder so many of us are turning to Costco. Everyone knows the warehouse is a deal machine for electronics, home goods, and tires, but this time of year, the aisles are also stocked with a surprising array of ski gear at steep discounts.

Plenty of skiers assume outdoor gear from substantial-box stores and other non-specialty retailers can’t be trusted. At Costco, that’s not necessarily true. The warehouse pulls in items from brands skiers know, like Smith, Spyder, Dakine, Eddie Bauer, and Head, and its seasoned members know a steal when they see one. A Spyder full-zip sweater jacket for $30 or less? That goes straight in the cart. Buy now, try on at home: Costco’s “satisfaction guaranteed” return policy means you can easily take back whatever doesn’t work out.

According to recent reports, the catch: buying ski gear from a warehouse means making compromises. A specialty ski shop has gear with premium features like name-brand insulation and weatherproof materials (and premium prices to match). If you’re outside for hours in gnarly weather, you may need those technical features to stay warm and dry. But casual skiers, beginners, and kids will find plenty of choices at Costco, and experts can find some gems, too. It’s the perfect place for a comfy fleece, a reasonably priced heated vest, a MIPS helmet, affordable gloves and goggles, and après-ski accessories. SKI recommends the following items, but act fast because, like a powder day, the goods won’t last.

Fine print: you’ll need a Costco membership to snag any of these, so factor the annual fee into your budget.

Smith is a specialty-shop staple, so finding the Survey on the Costco website is a legit surprise. This all-mountain lid pairs MIPS with Koroyd zones that keep the weight down. An integrated ChromaPop visor stands in for goggles and works with glasses, and a dial fine-tunes the fit.

According to recent reports, compromise: There really isn’t one. You get a top-shelf helmet at Costco pricing (it retails for around $260 elsewhere). If you weren’t a visor-helmet person before now, maybe you just became one?

According to recent reports, this is the budget way to get a MIPS-equipped helmet on your head, and it hits the feature checklist. Three-stage vents let you dump heat on sunny laps, the earpads come out when spring arrives, and a built-in goggle lock keeps most goggles from sliding off the back. An adjustable retention system helps dial in the fit, and it comes in four sizes, small through extra large.

Compromise: You get the safety and venting, but not the luxe features of a premium helmet, like a plush lining or a magnetic chin buckle.

In a recent development, magnetic lens swap systems are usually a perk of pricier goggles, but Nordik includes one in these affordable goggles. The HOD’s magnetic system lets you pop lenses in and out in seconds, and the box includes a second, low-light lens so you’re covered when the sun disappears. The oversized spherical lens has anti-fog treatment and UV400 protection, and the roomy OTG frame fits over large glasses and runs medium to large. A carrying case is thrown in, too.

Compromise: You’re not getting top-of-the-line lenses with light-adapting tech, so you’ll swap lenses by hand when conditions change.

When it comes to ski mittens, leather is king, and getting a deerskin outer at Costco prices is a serious bargain. Deerskin naturally sheds water and wind and holds up to season after season of abuse, the kind of toughness synthetic shells struggle to match. These pair that shell with 150-gram 3M Thinsulate and a waterproof, breathable insert. The extended gauntlet cuff, with an adjustable strap and cinch cord, seals out powder.

Compromise: You’re not getting a branded waterproof membrane like Gore-Tex, so don’t count on premium storm performance.

According to recent reports, you can outfit the entire family with Head’s ski gloves thanks to a size run ranging from XS to XL. With a combination of lightweight and breathable insulation and a waterproof/windproof insert, the gloves keep hands warm on milder ski days, with an exterior zippered pocket for handwarmers. Touchscreen technology means you can access your smartphone without removing your gloves.

In a recent development, compromise: If you spend less than $25 on gloves, don’t expect them to hold up to prolonged exposure to super cold temps or wet weather. (You’d have to spend at least $100 more for that.) Durability may be a weakness too, as the soft polyester material on the palm could peel off with use.

Recent findings suggest that dakine, born in Hawaii in 1979 and now a fixture in ski and snowboard shops, is another name you won’t expect to find next to the paper towels. This insulated midweight jacket has the details kids actually use: an inner powder skirt, a storm shield inside the hood, and two zippered side pockets. The hood comes off when it’s not needed, and sizes run XS–XL for the growth spurts that make buying premium kids’ gear hurt.

Pair it with the snow pants for a budget head-to-toe outfit. The insulated pants are wind and water resistant, with snow gaiters and elastic grippers that keep boots from letting in snow, plus a Velcro-adjustable waist for the in-between sizes. Two front slant pockets, a side zip pocket and scuff guards at the hems round it out.

Industry observers note that compromise: With the jacket, you’re giving up the proven weather protection of a premium kids’ shell. The jacket lists no waterproof rating or sealed seams, so think dry-snow resort days, not PNW storm skiing. For the pants, water resistant isn’t waterproof, so don’t count on these for skiing and playing in wet snow.

Eddie Bauer has been making outdoor clothing and gear since 1920, when Eddie Bauer opened his Sports Shop in Seattle, close to Costco’s headquarters in Washington. The hooded full-zip fleece nods to the days when a heavyweight midlayer doubled as a jacket. Layered under a shell for ski days, or standalone, the 100 percent polyester fleece has a soft and comfy kid-friendly hand feel.

Compromise: This isn’t a lightweight performance fleece for easy layering under a ski jacket; its heavyweight fuzzy fabric makes it better suited to après play and around-town wear.

At $50, the 32 Degrees Rechargeable Heated Vest is your gateway into heated ski gear. It’s the perfect marriage of value and warmth, and fits well over base and midlayers. Fleece-lined and lightweight, the vest comes pre-wired with four heat panels, two in front and two in back. A palm-sized battery pack, rechargeable through a USB-C charging cable, powers the heat, offering a little extra warmth for chilly chairlift rides.

Recent findings suggest that compromise: If you pay under $50, don’t expect the design and functionality of a $150 vest. Expect relatively short battery life, and make sure to research how to turn it on. Plus, all your friends will know when you have your vest turned on thanks to a red “Heat” logo. But embrace this: You will be warmer than them.

Recent findings suggest that 32 Degrees’ mission is to provide value and comfort, which is exactly why Costco skiers should take a hard look at the 32 Degrees Women’s Fleece. The high-pile fleece is not only soft and comfy, but it traps in body heat, while the 1/4-zip offers some venting. The kangaroo pocket doubles as a handwarmer, but what women may appreciate most is that the round-bottom hem looks cool with tights or snowpants.

Compromise: The sleeves are known to run long.

Spyder, founded in 1978 in Boulder, Colorado, is one of the most recognizable ski brands around the world. The Spyder Full Zip Sweater Jacket remains the quintessential ski town staple around every ski resort. Wear it as a standalone piece, or use the durable, heavyweight jacket as a midlayer under a ski jacket. Burly zippers abound with the full front zippered closure, a chest pocket and side storage pocket.

Sources indicate that compromise: The heavyweight fabric on this sweater jacket makes it a bit hefty for aerobic activities. Since it leans more après than technical, don’t expect great wind protection or core warmth.

Sources indicate that create a cool vibe during your après-ski tailgate with the Soundcore Boom 3i Outdoor Bluetooth speaker. Even if snowflakes fall, the waterproof and dustproof speaker keeps the beat without worrying about the elements. The rechargeable battery comes with a USB-C cable and holds a charge for up to 16 hours. At the end of a great ski day, the beat-synced lightshow hypes you up for more.

Industry observers note that compromise: There isn’t one. You get a tough, waterproof speaker at a reasonable price. It’s not a premium speaker for audiophiles, but it will get the job done.

One of the best feelings in life is taking off your ski boots and sliding your feet into something comfortable. Enter the Kirkland Signature Unisex Slipper. Kirkland, Costco’s signature brand, named for the Seattle suburb where Costco began, is not to be scoffed at because it often stands in for other more expensive brand-name items like Uggs. Case in point—the Shearling Slipper features genuine sheepskin shearling, an embroidered collar and a lightweight outsole grippy enough for mountain hut floors or ski area parking lots.

According to recent reports, compromise: You get the shearling-lined comfort of a premium slipper like an Ugg, but not the sole. Kirkland’s outsole is lightweight, so these are for hut floors and well-maintained parking lots.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (912 w)

Why Hunting Mallards in Flooded Timber is So Great

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best thing about timber hunting is the way ducks multiply.
  • It can build until you’ve got flocks working at two or three levels, and there’s less need for calling than there is for air traffic control.
  • Two drakes peel off the bunch and backpedal into the hole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best thing about timber hunting is the way ducks multiply. A pair starts to circle, and that pair becomes four, then eight. Eight turn into 20. Somehow, the sight of ducks working over a timber hole draws more ducks from everywhere. It’s almost like squirrels running out onto branches to see what the others are chattering about.

It can build until you’ve got flocks working at two or three levels, and there’s less need for calling than there is for air traffic control. I’ve seen that in Arkansas, but we won’t see it here—in a duck-poor state a couple hundred miles north. The two dozen mallards wheeling over our heads are as good as it’s going to get. But from where we stand, pressed tight to the trees, two dozen is more than good enough. ­Editor-​in-​chief Colin Kearns and I are doing that thing where you look down but roll your eyes up, trying to peek at ducks without flaring them, and our hearts are beating fast.

Two drakes peel off the bunch and backpedal into the hole. Travis Mueller, a Banded pro staffer, tells us not to shoot. He’s hoping the rest will follow. Kearns and I nod our heads—imperceptibly, we hope—and hold our guns ready. The rest of the ducks make one more circle, but higher and looser. Then they slide away. With the birds in the sky gone, we settle for the two in the bush. Jumping the two drakes, ­Kearns and I each shoot one. While we wish the rest had come in, the sight of these two in the trees, hanging over the decoys and lit by the morning sun, makes Kearns an instant convert to woods hunting.

Recent findings suggest that mueller, who scouts as hard as anyone, found this spot in spring by looking for beavers. Beavers plus woods equals flooded timber anywhere, and we’re standing in knee-deep water in the soft maples and willows growing between a couple of oxbow ponds. Mueller hunts here to get away from the crowds on the big water, but crowds have a habit of following successful hunters.

In a recent development, the first rule of timber hunting: No one talks about timber hunting. Good hunters are secretive. Mueller is a great hunter, so it’s no surprise he’s long since crossed the line from secretive to completely paranoid. We left the ramp extra early this morning to avoid detection. Even so, Mueller fretted the whole way that a couple of kids he thinks are watching him might have found his spot.

When we got to the hole, Mueller was sure his enemies were onto him. Three hundred mallards that had been sitting here yesterday weren’t here; someone must have run them out. And the decoys were missing—no doubt, in Mueller’s mind, stolen by the competition. As Kearns and I found fallen trunks for our gear, Mueller was looking for the bag of decoys he had stashed. We could hear him sloshing and cursing in the darkness.

In traditional flooded green timber, a lack of decoys wouldn’t be a problem. Old-school hunters in Arkansas relied on calling and ripples kicked in the water to attract ducks and went without decoys. Here, though, decoys and spinners are an advantage. There are no acorns to attract ducks. Birds don’t come to flooded soft woods to eat. They want a place to hide out and loaf. The ducks we’re after are trading back and forth between a couple of refuges, or coming back to the woods after feeding in the cornfields. They need enticement. In the words of a famous timber hunter: “There are two places you can kill a duck. Where he wants to be, and where he don’t mind goin’.” This is a don’t-mind-goin’ spot, hence, the need for decoys and spinners.

In a recent development, when Mueller finally shines his flashlight in the right place, he finds the decoy bag. The hole is still secret. In fact, we’ll see no other hunters nor hear any shots but our own this morning. Those 300 mallards? Who knows. They were probably fresh arrivals that dropped in, then found other ducks and relocated.

With two dozen decoys in the hole and four spinners going, we’re looking good. Spinners work well in the woods, Mueller believes, because ducks lose sight of them, then see them again, as they pass over the latticework of branches. And the sun is shining. “Sun’s out, guns out” is a truism of timber hunting. Decoys show up, spinners flash, and the sun creates shadows that make it easy to hide beside a tree.

According to recent reports, mueller blind-calls, quacking at random intervals to whom it may concern. Often in timber hunting, you don’t see the ducks you’re calling or decoying until after they have seen you. We’re not aware of the flock until we hear the whoosh of wings overhead. When the birds drop in I miss, Kearns kills a greenhead, and Mueller shoots a bluewing drake, fully plumed, unheard of at this latitude with 10 days left in the season. It’s been a strange migration year.

In a recent development, we peck away at a few more, and call it a morning, being careful to pick up our hulls both because it’s what you do, and to hide any sign of our presence. For good measure, we pack the decoys out, too. A flooded hole in the woods is worth keeping secret.

The Rules of Trail Running Etiquette, from the ATRA President

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners.
  • To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other owners.
  • Those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners. And as a six-decade trail veteran myself, I also know a little about the improper behavior of trail runners.

To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other owners.

Those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect. Here are the basics of what you should know when you hit the trails:.

Close any gates you open, don’t disturb the wildlife or livestock, and respect private land and get permission to enter.

Take only photos and pack out at least as much as you brought in, including gel wrappers. If needed, wear shorts, a jacket, or hydration pack with zip pockets to stow rubbish found on the trail.

According to recent reports, don’t disturb wildlife as frightened animals may be dangerous. Steer clear of trails that disturb sensitive habitats during nesting or mating seasons. When passing horses, use special care and follow directions from the horseback riders. Consider turning around and going another direction when faced with large herds of animals.

Don’t play your music loudly, engage in boisterous conversations with your fellow runners (or through speakerphone), or listen to headphones so loudly that you are unaware of your surroundings. Along the same lines, do your social media influencing elsewhere. Nature is not your recording studio. We don’t want to hear you, and you ought to be able to hear others.

We expect the same of cyclists. This should be obvious but, then again, all of this should be.

As trail runners, we move relatively promptly, especially when we seemingly emerge from nowhere on unsuspecting trail customers. This may be alarming, so anticipate and give a courteous and audible announcement of your presence and intention to pass hikers on the trail by stating something along the lines of, “On your left,” or “Trail,” as you approach. Keep an eye out for those wearing headphones, as they won’t hear your warning. Be courteous when passing, slowing down or stopping if necessary to prevent accidental contact. Be ready to yield to all other trail users (cyclists, hikers, horses) even if you have the posted right of way.

It has been revealed that this is likely to be controversial, but consider not bringing your dog on group runs and, when you do run with your dogs, be sure to leash them and keep them under your control when necessary to prevent any wildlife disturbances. Be sure to pack out their (and your) waste.

Be cognizant that off-leash dogs often chase wildlife and degrade the outdoor experience of other trail customers.

In a recent development, greet and say “Excuse me” to those you see and pass on the trail. This should be a common practice if for no other reason than to alert others to your presence and not frighten anyone. Similarly, be sure to stay in control of your speed, especially when you could cause rocks or other trail features to fall.

In a recent development, if you startle someone, apologize, and thank them if they’ve stepped aside. A little kindness goes a long way on the trail.

Don’t cut the switchbacks or widen trails by running around puddles,downed trees, or when it is too muddy.

Don’t create your own trails by running off preexisting, well-marked trails. When multiple trails exist, run on the most worn. Stay off closed trails and obey all postings.

Run single file in the middle of a trail, even if it’s laden with a fresh blanket of snow or thick mud. Go over, not around, obstacles like puddles,rocks, or downed tree limbs, as that widens trails, damages vegetation, and causes unnecessary erosion.

In other words, participate in trail maintenance and give back to the trail community.

In a now-infamous Outside opinion piece of seven years ago that went viral, Marc Peruzzi claimed that trail runners are lazy parasites. Ultrarunner and lawyer Stephanie Case wrote a response piece, saying more could be done, agreeing with my stance that “we are guilty as charged … we need [to do] more. A lot more.” Case continued, “Indeed, as trail running continues to increase in popularity, it will become even more vital that we expand our volunteer and conservation efforts.”.

So, carry your weight and do trail work. Volunteer. Go plogging on your local trails.

Sources indicate that technically, those ascending are supposed to have the right of way but, in practice, people often yield to descenders, likely due to speed and momentum. Be polite, maintain control, and be prepared to yield to other people, including horseback riders.

Split larger groups into smaller groups as bigger numbers can intimidate other owners and have a greater environmental impact on trails.

If you come across someone in distress, stop and check whether they need help.

Recent findings suggest that don’t become a liability by taking risks, getting lost, or ignoring trail closures that require dangerous rescues. Carry proper clothing, nutrition, and hydration so as not to put yourself at risk of exposure. Safety first is always a good rule.

If running alone, familiarize yourself with the area where you initiative to run and let at least one other person know your intended route. Be prepared for the weather and conditions when you start your run and plan for the worst, given the likely duration of your run. Know and respect your limits and report unsafe conditions and activities to the proper authorities.

Sources indicate that trail running is beautifully simple. So is being a courteous trail runner. Follow these tips for proper etiquette and keep the trails safe, welcoming, and wild!

#136372. Industry News: 5 Steps To Taking An Elk With An Over-The-Counter Tag

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2154 w)

Industry News: 5 Steps To Taking An Elk With An Over-The-Counter Tag

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that over-the-counter (OTC) elk units tend to get a bad rap.
  • Recent findings suggest that the good news: OTC units can produce incredible hunting for elk if you follow these guidelines.
  • Sources indicate that locating OTC elk units, thanks to newly polished western game and fish websites, is a breeze.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that over-the-counter (OTC) elk units tend to get a bad rap. It doesn’t matter, either, if the particular unit boasts unlimited tags or those offered on a first-come basis. Most hunters will be quick to sneer at them. Of course, hunting pressure in OTC units is going to be higher than those found in coveted draw units. Elk encounters may be fewer, and made-by-elk vocalizations may be hard to come by. However, if the thought of going years (sometimes decades) in between guttural bugles and basins littered with golden aspens disgusts you, OTC units need to become your best friend. Successful OTC elk hunting, whether you’re toting a bow or rifle, comes down to having a system for success. The following advice applies to both crowds. If you put it to practice, a date with an OTC bull is likely in the coming weeks and months.

Recent findings suggest that the good news: OTC units can produce incredible hunting for elk if you follow these guidelines. Forget the odds and the naysayers. If you’re willing to work hard and be relentless, good things will happen. Colorado boasts the world’s largest elk population (just north of 280,000 animals) and gives resident and nonresident bowhunters a total of 137 out of 184 units to chase their OTC elk dreams in—we are going to refer to it often.

Sources indicate that locating OTC elk units, thanks to newly polished western game and fish websites, is a breeze. Idaho, for instance, provides OTC tags on a first-come basis in all but one of its elk management zones and all but three of its elk management units. Naturally, popular units go fast, so do your research and be ready to go when those units go on sale. Colorado, on the other hand, offers unlimited tags in its OTC units, and tags can be purchased starting in early August through the end of the season. Colorado’s OTC units are easily discovered by simply looking at the regulation’s brochure. These units are highlighted and clearly marked.

Industry observers note that when looking for a prospective OTC elk unit, the first thing I like to do is check out hunter success. Yes, I realize these percentage rates are often skewed due to bowhunters who don’t hunt at all, hunt only a day or two, or never leave the comfort of their Chevy, however, I do believe they have a lot of value. If you can locate a hunt unit or better yet a trio or more that have connecting borders that boast success rates above 10 percent, they are worth a look. Most western states ask hunters to fill out surveys at the end of the season, and results are then posted to the state’s game and fish website. Take advantage. While you’re looking at success rates, it’s also a good idea to peek at recent population counts and bull-to-cow ratios. Again, most every western state will have this information on their website. I like to print out success rates, population, and bull-to-cow ratio sheets and use them to triangulate a likely hunt unit.

Industry observers note that don’t disregard isolated single units either, especially if they border draw units. I’ve had some great hunts pressing in close to a draw-unit area and hunting the border. The biggest reason I like connecting units is if I’m struggling to find elk, I don’t like to wait around. Elk are significant travelers. If I spend a full day hunting an area and don’t see a single elk, hear a bugle or at the very least see some greasy sign, I bounce. If you do opt to put all of your OTC eggs into a single unit, be sure that unit has plenty of National Forest and BLM access, which takes us to Step 2.

Recent findings suggest that now that you have a few units in mind, it’s time to pull those units up on your onX Hunt App. If you don’t have onX, get it. Not only does this digital mapping system allow you to mark likely hunt locales, but it also shows public/private land boundaries and is loaded with an abundance of other helpful features like hunt unit boundaries and the like.

In a recent development, what are you looking for? Access for starters. I like to locate off-the-beaten-path areas that require a mile or more jaunt to get into them and are restricted to travel on foot, horseback, or pedal power. If you can locate a trail snaking through vast acres of public land with no other road access available for miles around, take note of it. In addition to locating off-the-beaten-path locations, you’ll also want to mark between eight and 10 (the more, the better) right-off-the-road areas. No, I’m not crazy. The go-deep drum has been beaten hard, which has increased competition in the backcountry and left piles of easy-access spots abandoned. Locate areas right off of a main road that dive into a hellish bottom or require a long, vertical walk. Both will discourage the masses. A pair of my hunting partners have utilized this off-the-road tactic over the past two seasons in Colorado. The results have been four public-land bulls over a total of 10 hunt days, and my amigos slept in the comfort of their camper each night.

Sources indicate that it’s also a good idea, especially once you’ve decided on a hunt unit, to get a good paper topo map. I prefer those from HuntData due to the fact that they are printed on Dura-Map fabric, which stands up against weather and in-and-out-of-pack abuse.

Sources indicate that with your hunt area pulled up on onX maps and your paper map in hand, it’s time to look for likely elk haunts. If the plan is to pack in deep and seek secluded areas, remember that elk need water, cover, and food. The more rugged the country, the better. Any areas with deep drainages lined by steep slopes should be noted. These drainages offer thick bedding cover, and streams often trickle down their middles. Other areas of interest should be steep country that levels out on large benches (long, flat spots amidst steep country) before dropping off once again. Elk love to rut on benches. Other notable spots include small, secluded meadows in the middle of a sea of deep, dark timber. Elk will feed in these meadows early and late, and most will contain at least one well-used wallow.

If your destination is Colorado, don’t overlook units with wilderness areas inside their boundaries. In Colorado, both residents and non-residents can access wilderness areas without a guide, and these locations are usually the best recipe for getting away from people and experiencing a true backcountry hunt. Travel into wilderness areas is limited to foot and horseback only. Simplify your OTC unit/wilderness area search by visiting coloradowilderness.com.

Read Next: Elk Hunting Archery Tactics for Post-Rut Bulls.

According to recent reports, what about north-facing slopes? Sure, north-facing slopes are good for bedding, but over the years, especially during the rut, I don’t worry at all about which direction a slope faces. I go where the elk are.

Recent findings suggest that if you like the dive-off-the-road plan or want to use it as a backup if your go-deep idea goes to crap, again, look for areas that drop promptly in elevation. Elk will hold up in deep dark holes. Another option, and one my hunting partners and I use a lot, is the straight-up approach. If you can find some off-the-road vert that leads to a good bench, mark it. The more spots you have marked, the more you can bounce in and out of. Another great tactic is to look at easy-access areas that will draw the masses, and then located the nastiest, steepest area in close proximity to these areas. These locations will often fill up with pressured elk. Remember, it takes only one bull to cooperate.

Industry observers note that I know it’s been written about more times than Gene Simmons has flicked his tongue at Kiss concert, but it’s really a must do. Call the local state game and fish office nearest your hunt locale and get the number for the area biologist. I love these folks. Why? Simple, they spend most all of their time in the field compiling data, and most everyone of them I’ve ever talked to is dying to share it with a source other than a spreadsheet.

The trick is to honor their time. If you’re lucky enough to get them on the phone, have a list of pre-prepared questions written down. They will appreciate this and will be more apt to provide helpful information. Chances are, however, you won’t get them on the phone. No biggie. Leave a message and they will call you back. The problem is they will call you back while you’re checking out of the grocery store or at some other inopportune time—mark my words. For this reason, I carry my list of questions in my wallet. This way I have my questions on-hand at all times. Here is a quick list to get you started. Feel free to add your own.

According to recent reports, these are the areas I’m looking at. Can you recommend any others where I may be able to get away from people and find elk?

Have there been any winter mortality challenges or any other factors in the area that have led to a recent population decline?

Are there any special camping or hunting rules in this location that I need to be aware of?

How have calf survival rates been over the past few years?

Is there anything you know of that should discourage me from hunting this area?

From a biologist’s point of view, what about any encouraging factors?

According to recent reports, sadly, it’s this step that most don’t complete—and those that do won’t follow the advice to come. You’ve done the research and are all ready to go, so, please, go! Many would-be elk hunters, after they’ve done all the leg work, simply don’t go. They talk themselves out of the idea and listen to reports from naysayers who’ve had “bad” OTC experiences. Remember, most of these experiences were the sole fault of the participant. I had a guy tell me last year at a sporting goods store that he hadn’t heard a bugle in 10 days of hunting. He was hunting the same general area my hunting partners and I were, and we’d heard multiple bugles each day and killed a pair of bulls. The difference: He expected the unit to be like an elk hunting video. He was driving access roads and trying to solicit bugles from his truck. This leads us into the second half of Step 5.

It’s essential that you go into your hunt with realistic expectations. Unless you end up on a bench with a handful of hot cows and a number of satellite bulls circling the girls with herd bull trying to protect his harem, it’s likely you won’t hear the type of bugling you’ll see on outdoor television. Remember, you’re hunting pressured land and elk that have likely been called to. Lots of bulls come in silent to bull and cow talk.

Another important tip (especially if this is your maiden voyage into the elk woods) is to have realistic expectations when it comes to the size of your harvest. I live in Colorado, and unless I have a draw tag in my pocket, I shoot the first legal bull I see. This takes the pressure off and typically allows me to fill my freezer with meat. Most Colorado OTC units offer either-sex licenses, and there have been many seasons where I slammed a broadhead-tipped arrow through a tasty cow.

Recent findings suggest that go into the hunt with the mindset that you will shoot the first legal elk you’ll see, and it will be that much more enjoyable. I also recommend, especially if this is your first trip into an area, to simply focus your hunt around learning your unit. Learn and take note of your access points. Keep notes about elk encounters and the like. The goal is just to get into elk. If you find a place void of people and teeming with elk, you’ve found a gem you can go back to on those years you don’t have a draw tag in your wallet.

Industry observers note that with seasons open across the West, Colorado may be your best option. When it comes to a few units to help jumpstart your search, look to those in the states Northwest and Southwest. A few with connecting borders include 11, 21, and 22 as well as 80, 81, and 78.

It has been revealed that there you have it. All the info you need to go OTC. Get after it!
